In [[set theory]] and [[Mathematical logic|logic]], '''Buchholz's ID hierarchy''' is a hierarchy of subsystems of [[Peano axioms|first-order arithmetic]]. The systems/theories <math>\mathsf{ID}_\nu</math> are referred to as "the formal theories of ''ν''-times iterated inductive definitions". ID<sub>''ν''</sub> extends [[Peano axioms|PA]] by ''ν'' iterated least fixed points of [[monotone operator]]s.

== Definition ==

=== Original definition ===
The formal theory ID<sub>ω</sub> (and ID<sub>''ν''</sub> in general) is an extension of [[Peano axioms|Peano Arithmetic]], formulated in the language L<sub>ID</sub>, by the following axioms:<ref>W. Buchholz, "An Independence Result for <math>(\Pi^1_1\textrm{-CA})\textrm{+BI}</math>", [[Annals of Pure and Applied Logic]] vol. 33 (1987).</ref>
* <math>\forall y \forall x (\mathfrak{M}_y(P^\mathfrak{M}_y, x) \rightarrow x \in P^\mathfrak{M}_y)</math>
* <math>\forall y (\forall x (\mathfrak{M}_y(F, x) \rightarrow F(x)) \rightarrow \forall x (x \in P^\mathfrak{M}_y \rightarrow F(x)))</math> for every L<sub>ID</sub>-formula F(x)
* <math>\forall y \forall x_0 \forall x_1(P^\mathfrak{M}_{<y}x_0x_1 \leftrightarrow x_0 < y \land x_1 \in P^\mathfrak{M}_{x_0})</math>

The theory ID<sub>ν</sub> with ν ≠ ω is defined as:
* <math>\forall y \forall x (Z_y(P^\mathfrak{M}_y, x) \rightarrow x \in P^\mathfrak{M}_y)</math>
* <math>\forall x (\mathfrak{M}_u(F, x) \rightarrow F(x)) \rightarrow \forall x (P^\mathfrak{M}_ux \rightarrow F(x))</math> for every L<sub>ID</sub>-formula F(x) and each u < ν
* <math>\forall y \forall x_0 \forall x_1(P^\mathfrak{M}_{<y}x_0x_1 \leftrightarrow x_0 < y \land x_1 \in P^\mathfrak{M}_{x_0})</math>

=== Explanation / alternate definition ===

==== ID<sub>1</sub> ====
A set <math>I \subseteq \N</math> is called inductively defined if for some monotonic operator <math>\Gamma: P(N) \rightarrow P(N)</math>, <math>LFP(\Gamma) = I</math>, where <math>LFP(f)</math> denotes the [[least fixed point]] of <math>f</math>. The language of ID<sub>1</sub>, <math>L_{ID_1}</math>, is obtained from that of first-order number theory, <math>L_\N</math>, by the addition of a set (or predicate) constant I<sub>A</sub> for every X-positive formula A(X, x) in L<sub>N</sub>[X] that only contains X (a new set variable) and x (a number variable) as free variables. The term X-positive means that X only occurs positively in A (X is never on the left of an implication). We allow ourselves a bit of set-theoretic notation:

* <math>F = \{x \in N \mid F(x)\}</math>
* <math>s \in F</math> means <math>F(s)</math>
* For two formulas <math>F</math> and <math>G</math>, <math>F \subseteq G</math> means <math>\forall x F(x) \rightarrow G(x)</math>.

Then ID<sub>1</sub> contains the axioms of first-order number theory (PA) with the induction scheme extended to the new language as well as these axioms:

* <math>(ID_1)^1: A(I_A) \subseteq I_A</math>
* <math>(ID_1)^2: A(F) \subseteq F \rightarrow I_A \subseteq F</math>

Where <math>F(x)</math> ranges over all <math>L_{ID_1}</math> formulas.

Note that <math>(ID_1)^1</math> expresses that <math>I_A</math> is closed under the arithmetically [[definable set]] operator <math>\Gamma_A(S) = \{x \in \N \mid \N \models A(S, x)\}</math>, while <math>(ID_1)^2</math> expresses that <math>I_A</math> is the least such (at least among sets definable in <math>L_{ID_1}</math>).

Thus, <math>I_A</math> is meant to be the least pre-fixed-point, and hence the least fixed point of the operator <math>\Gamma_A</math>.

==== ID<sub>ν</sub> ====
To define the system of ν-times iterated inductive definitions, where ν is an ordinal, let <math>\prec</math> be a primitive recursive well-ordering of [[order type]] ν. We use Greek letters to denote elements of the field of <math>\prec</math>. The language of ID<sub>ν</sub>, <math>L_{ID_\nu}</math> is obtained from <math>L_\N</math> by the addition of a binary predicate constant J<sub>A</sub> for every X-positive <math>L_\N[X, Y]</math> formula <math>A(X, Y, \mu, x)</math> that contains at most the shown free variables, where X is again a unary (set) variable, and Y is a fresh binary [[predicate variable]]. We write <math>x \in J^\mu_A</math> instead of <math>J_A(\mu, x)</math>, thinking of x as a distinguished variable in the latter formula.

The system ID<sub>ν</sub> is now obtained from the system of first-order number theory (PA) by expanding the induction scheme to the new language and adding the scheme <math>(TI_\nu): TI(\prec, F)</math> expressing [[transfinite induction]] along <math>\prec</math> for an arbitrary <math>L_{ID_\nu}</math> formula <math>F</math> as well as the axioms:

* <math>(ID_\nu)^1: \forall \mu \prec \nu; A^\mu(J^\mu_A) \subseteq J^\mu_A</math>
* <math>(ID_\nu)^2: \forall \mu \prec \nu; A^\mu(F) \subseteq F \rightarrow J^\mu_A \subseteq F</math>

where <math>F(x)</math> is an arbitrary <math>L_{ID_\nu}</math> formula. In <math>(ID_\nu)^1</math> and <math>(ID_\nu)^2</math> we used the abbreviation <math>A^\mu(F)</math> for the formula <math>A(F, (\lambda\gamma y; \gamma \prec \mu \land y \in J^\gamma_A), \mu, x)</math>, where <math>x</math> is the distinguished variable. We see that these express that each <math>J^\mu_A</math>, for <math>\mu \prec \nu</math>, is the least fixed point (among definable sets) for the operator <math>\Gamma^\mu_A(S) = \{n \in \N | (\N, (J^\gamma_A)_{\gamma \prec \mu}\}</math>. Note how all the previous sets <math>J^\gamma_A</math>, for <math>\gamma \prec \mu</math>, are used as parameters.

We then define <math display="inline">ID_{\prec \nu} = \bigcup _{\xi \prec \nu}ID_\xi</math>.

==== Variants ====
<math>\widehat{\mathsf{ID}}_\nu</math> - <math>\widehat{\mathsf{ID}}_\nu</math> is a weakened version of <math>\mathsf{ID}_\nu</math>. In the system of <math>\widehat{\mathsf{ID}}_\nu</math>, a set <math>I \subseteq \N</math> is instead called inductively defined if for some monotonic operator <math>\Gamma: P(N) \rightarrow P(N)</math>, <math>I</math> is a fixed point of <math>\Gamma</math>, rather than the least fixed point. This subtle difference makes the system significantly weaker: <math>PTO(\widehat{\mathsf{ID}}_1) = \psi(\Omega^{\varepsilon_0})</math>, while <math>PTO(\mathsf{ID}_1) = \psi(\varepsilon_{\Omega+1})</math>.

<math>\mathsf{ID}_\nu\#</math> is <math>\widehat{\mathsf{ID}}_\nu</math> weakened even further. In <math>\mathsf{ID}_\nu\#</math>, not only does it use fixed points rather than least fixed points, and has induction only for positive formulas. This once again subtle difference makes the system even weaker: <math>PTO(\mathsf{ID}_1\#) = \psi(\Omega^\omega) </math>, while <math>PTO(\widehat{\mathsf{ID}}_1) = \psi(\Omega^{\varepsilon_0})</math>.

<math>\mathsf{W-ID}_\nu</math> is the weakest of all variants of <math>\mathsf{ID}_\nu</math>, based on W-types. The amount of weakening compared to regular iterated inductive definitions is identical to removing [[bar induction]] given a certain subsystem of [[second-order arithmetic]]. <math>PTO(\mathsf{W-ID}_1) = \psi_0(\Omega\times\omega) </math>, while <math>PTO(\mathsf{ID}_1) = \psi(\varepsilon_{\Omega+1})</math>.

<math>\mathsf{U(ID}_\nu\mathsf{)}</math> is an "unfolding" strengthening of <math>\mathsf{ID}_\nu</math>. It is not exactly a first-order arithmetic system, but captures what one can get by predicative reasoning based on ν-times iterated generalized inductive definitions. The amount of increase in strength is identical to the increase from <math>\varepsilon_0</math> to <math>\Gamma_0</math>: <math>PTO(\mathsf{ID}_1) = \psi(\varepsilon_{\Omega+1})</math>, while <math>PTO(\mathsf{U(ID}_1\mathsf{)}) = \psi(\Gamma_{\Omega+1}) </math>.

== Results ==
* Let ν > 0. If a ∈ T<sub>0</sub> contains no symbol D<sub>μ</sub> with ν < μ, then "a ∈ W<sub>0</sub>" is provable in ID<sub>ν</sub>.
* ID<sub>ω</sub> is contained in <math>\Pi^1_1 - CA + BI</math>.
* If a <math>\Pi^0_2</math>-sentence <math>\forall x \exists y \varphi(x, y) (\varphi \in \Sigma^0_1)</math> is provable in ID<sub>ν</sub>, then there exists <math>p \in N</math> such that <math>\forall n \geq p \exists k < H_{D_0D^n_\nu0}(1) \varphi(n, k)</math>.
* If the sentence A is provable in ID<sub>ν</sub> for all ν < ω, then there exists k ∈ N such that <math>\vdash_k^{D^k_\nu0} A^N</math>.

== Proof-theoretic ordinals ==

* The proof-theoretic ordinal of ID<sub><ν</sub> is equal to <math>\psi_0(\Omega_\nu)</math>.
* The proof-theoretic ordinal of ID<sub>ν</sub> is equal to <math>\psi_0(\varepsilon_{\Omega_\nu+1}) = \psi_0(\Omega_{\nu+1})</math> .
* The proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>\widehat{ID}_{<\omega}</math> is equal to <math>\Gamma_0</math>.
* The proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>\widehat{ID}_\nu</math> for <math>\nu < \omega</math> is equal to <math>\varphi(\varphi(\nu, 0), 0)</math>.
* The proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>\widehat{ID}_{\varphi(\alpha, \beta)}</math> is equal to <math>\varphi(1, 0, \varphi(\alpha+1, \beta-1))</math>.
* The proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>\widehat{ID}_{<\varphi(0, \alpha)}</math> for <math>\alpha > 1</math> is equal to <math>\varphi(1, \alpha, 0)</math>.
* The proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>\widehat{ID}_{<\nu}</math> for <math>\nu \geq \varepsilon_0</math> is equal to <math>\varphi(1, \nu, 0)</math>.
* The proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>ID_\nu\#</math> is equal to <math>\varphi(\omega^\nu, 0)</math>.
*The proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>ID_{<\nu}\#</math> is equal to <math>\varphi(0, \omega^{\nu+1})</math>.
* The proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>W\textrm{-}ID_{\varphi(\alpha, \beta)}</math> is equal to <math>\psi_0(\Omega_{\varphi(\alpha, \beta)}\times\varphi(\alpha+1, \beta-1))</math>.
*The proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>W\textrm{-}ID_{<\varphi(\alpha, \beta)}</math> is equal to <math>\psi_0(\varphi(\alpha+1, \beta-1)^{\Omega_{\varphi(\alpha, \beta-1)}+1})</math>.
* The proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>U(ID_\nu)</math> is equal to <math>\psi_0(\varphi(\nu, 0, \Omega+1))</math>.
*The proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>U(ID_{<\nu})</math> is equal to <math>\psi_0(\Omega^{\Omega+\varphi(\nu, 0, \Omega)})</math>.
* The proof-theoretic ordinal of ID<sub>1</sub> (the [[Bachmann–Howard ordinal|Bachmann-Howard ordinal]]) is also the proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>\mathsf{KP}</math>, <math>\mathsf{KP\omega}</math>, <math>\mathsf{CZF}</math> and <math>\mathsf{ML_{1}V}</math>.
* The proof-theoretic ordinal of W-ID<sub>ω</sub> (<math>\psi_0(\Omega_\omega\varepsilon_0)</math>) is also the proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>\mathsf{W-KPI}</math>.
* The proof-theoretic ordinal of ID<sub>ω</sub> (the [[Takeuti–Feferman–Buchholz ordinal|Takeuti-Feferman-Buchholz ordinal]]) is also the proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>\mathsf{KPI}</math>, <math>\Pi^1_1 - \mathsf{CA} + \mathsf{BI}</math> and <math>\Delta^1_2 - \mathsf{CA} + \mathsf{BI}</math>.
* The proof-theoretic ordinal of ID<sub><ω^ω</sub> (<math>\psi_0(\Omega_{\omega^\omega})</math>) is also the proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>\Delta^1_2 - \mathsf{CR}</math>.
* The proof-theoretic ordinal of ID<sub><ε0</sub> (<math>\psi_0(\Omega_{\varepsilon_0})</math>) is also the proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>\Delta^1_2 - \mathsf{CA}</math> and <math>\Sigma^1_2 - \mathsf{AC}</math>.
